schools.summary: Ellicott dates 'after these things' between 483 and 481 BC, the marriage delayed till after Xerxes' return from Greece; Keil and Delitzsch read the courtiers' proposal to seek a new queen.
Henry turns the notice into providence — God putting down the high Vashti and exalting the humble Esther (Magnificat, Hannah) — and the extravagant course taken to please a sensual king.
Gill dates the appeasing of the wrath after Xerxes' Greek campaign, the marriage in the seventh year.

themes: the search for a new queen

schools.summary: Gill: the servants advise partly from fear of Vashti's revenge, partly to lift the king's melancholy.
Clarke describes how an Eastern harem was furnished — the empire's fairest brought in, all concubines, one raised as sultana whose issue inherits.
Keil and Delitzsch give the proposal in full: virgins sought, officers, the house of the women, purification, the pleasing maiden made queen.
Henry weighs the pains taken to humour a sensual prince and the vile affections of those without revelation, yet bids us see the overruling grace.

Clarke reads 'chamberlain' as eunuch and the cosmetics as oil of myrrh and odours (with the Targum's oil of unripe olives); Wesley distinguishes Hege over the virgins from Shaashgaz over the concubines, the Jewish purification disregarded.
Ellicott names the house of the women the harem and distinguishes its keepers, and sees in it the degrading Eastern view of woman that Christianity would overturn.
Gill: the officers were those who knew where the fair virgins of each province were to be found.
Henry's scornful inventory — provinces searched, a house prepared, twelve months' purifying to help even nature's masterpieces to a carnal mind.
Gill: the royal estate and crown taken from Vashti pass to the maiden who pleases the king.
Keil and Delitzsch add the closing clauses — the thing pleased the king, and he did so.
Clarke: one is lifted above the rest as chief wife and sultana, her issue entitled to inherit.
Henry sees the overruling providence bringing Esther to the throne, and defends her honour (on Bishop Patrick) — every one the king took was married to him, a wife of lower rank, as Hagar to Abraham.
Ellicott (with Rawlinson) even identifies Mordecai with the eunuch Matacas and reads him as an ambitious worldling; Keil and Delitzsch simply set him in Shushan as Mordecai son of Jair, a Benjamite.
Gill explains why a Benjamite is called a Jew — he belonged to the kingdom of Judah, whose captives all bore the name.
Clarke reports the Targum's romance that Shimei was David's curser, spared to become Mordecai's ancestor.

debates.question: Was Mordecai a eunuch of the royal harem?

sides.position: an ordinary Jewish court official and faithful foster-father
probably a eunuch, identified with Matacas, from his free access to the harem

outliers.note: Reads Mordecai darkly as an ambitious, worldly man who preferred alien soil and calculated on his ward's beauty — a portrait the other witnesses and the later book do not share.

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch make Kish the antecedent carried away with Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) in 598 BC, a hundred and seventeen years and four generations back.
Gill argues the captivity attaches to Kish, not Mordecai, else Esther would be far too old to be a young and lovely maiden (the Targum's seventy-five not credible).
Keil and Delitzsch derive Esther from Old-Persian stara (star); Ellicott sees the common Jewish two-name practice (Saul/Paul) and names Abihail her father.
Clarke calls Hadassah her Babylonish name and Esther Persian, and insists she was Mordecai's cousin, not niece; Wesley notes Esther the name given by the king after marriage.
Gill glosses Hadassah as myrtle and Esther as 'star' or 'to hide,' and toys with the Amestris identification before recording the objections.
Henry draws the pathos — an orphan the Lord took up (Ps. 27:10), a beauty whose virtue was her greater beauty, a foster-child of Mordecai's kindness.
Keil and Delitzsch: the decree proclaimed, many maidens gathered to Shushan, Esther received into the harem under Hegai.
Clarke: Esther chosen among the young women and set under Hegai to begin the year of purifying.
Gill: the commandment and decree heard through the several provinces.
Henry: who would have thought a captive orphan born to be an empress? — Providence raising the poor from the dust (1 Sam. 2:8).

themes: the poor raised from the dust

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch list the favour Esther won — purification, portion, seven maidens, the best place; Ellicott hears in 'obtained kindness' the very phrase of the king's own favour at v.17.
Clarke credits her propriety and unassuming manners; Wesley traces the favour also to the divine power that moves men's hearts.
Gill: it was the chamberlain, not yet the king, whom her beauty and behaviour won.
Henry: wisdom and virtue gain respect, and those sure of God's favour find favour with men too.

themes: the seven maidens and the best place
favour given as well as earned

schools.summary: Clarke: a known Jewish birth might have prejudiced the king and roused envy; Wesley adds a hand of God in the concealment, unknown to Mordecai.
Keil and Delitzsch make the concealment the reason for her kind usage; Ellicott, Mordecai's hope she pass for a Persian, the king learning her nation only at Est 7:4.
Gill: unasked, and born in Shushan, she was taken for a native Persian.
Henry guards the ethics — not denying her country nor lying, only not proclaiming it: all truths need not be spoken at all times.

themes: hiding a truth without a lie

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: Mordecai walked daily to learn Esther's welfare, keeping unbroken communication; Ellicott infers he was a royal doorkeeper (cf. v.21; 5:13).
Gill: his post at court let him walk before the women's house unchallenged (Aben Ezra).
Henry: he was tender of her as his own child — let those given charge of kin be as solicitous.
Keil and Delitzsch fix the twelve months — six of myrrh, six of spices; Ellicott notes 'manner' is rather 'law' or 'ordinance' (Est 1:8).
Clarke ventures a physician's rationale — the year of diet, baths, and oil to sweeten the body-odour bred by coarse food.
Gill: each came in her turn after twelve months, as Herodotus reports of the Persian kings' wives.
Henry: art lavished on nature's masterpieces to please a vain and carnal mind.

outliers.note: Explains the year of purifying as hygiene and physic — diet, hot baths, and oil to remove the strong body-odour of those bred on coarse food — where the others see only luxury.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: whatever she asked given her; evening to the king, morning to the second house under Shaashgaz; no return unless called by name.
Clarke: any dress, colour, or jewels she chose were granted; Wesley: every one the king took was his wife of lower rank (as Hagar), so no dishonour to Esther.
Gill: thus came every virgin, her twelve months of purifying accomplished.
Keil and Delitzsch: in the morning to the second house, to Shaashgaz keeper of the concubines, no more to the king unless delighted in and called by name.
Clarke: the concubines went out no more, never married, unless summoned; Shaashgaz a Persian name for a eunuch.
Gill: the second apartment for the concubines (Aben Ezra, 'the second time').
Henry: recluses ever after, secondary wives forbidden to marry — the absurd practices of those without revelation.
Keil and Delitzsch: she required nothing but what Hegai appointed, and won favour of all who looked on her by modesty and humility.
Clarke: she left all to Hegai's judgment, going in only what he thought most suitable.
Gill names her the daughter of Abihail (not Aminadab as the LXX), Mordecai's cousin and foster-child.
Henry: not solicitous for artificial beauty, she asked for nothing — the more natural, the more agreeable — and won the prize.
Keil and Delitzsch date the taking to the tenth month Tebeth, seventh year; Ellicott sets it January-February 478 BC, just after Xerxes' return, the delay explained by the Greek war.
Clarke: Tebeth answers to part of our December and January.
Gill: Esther alone was retained as wife, not dismissed to the women's house like the concubines.
Henry: the seventh year, Vashti divorced in the third (Est 1:3) — four years without a queen, then a swift choice.
Keil and Delitzsch: from their first meeting the king loved Esther above all, set the crown on her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti.
Clarke: the crown made her the Sultana, mistress of all the wives, owed profound respect.
Gill: loved above all the women — the virgins made concubines, or, per Jarchi, married women too.
Henry: the king needed no further trial but was soon determined to crown her — the turn on which the providence swings.
Keil and Delitzsch read the 'release' as a holiday from labour, not a tax-remission (though the Chaldee took it of taxes); Ellicott, a release from tribute or military service, probably tribute.
Clarke: a remittance of tribute at the coronation, perhaps a relief of cities from the 'queen-gold.'
Gill: the marriage-feast, seven days (the Greek) or a whole month (Josephus).
Henry: a remission of tax arrears or an act of grace for criminals, as Pilate released a prisoner; Esther makes the appearance Vashti refused.

debates.question: What was the 'release' the king made to the provinces?

sides.position: a holiday, a release from labour
a remission of taxes or tribute
an act of grace releasing prisoners, or remitting tax arrears

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch own the second gathering obscure; Ellicott makes it evidence of how little the king's 'love' was worth, joining v.21 to this verse (Est 3:7).
Gill: not a backward reference to Vashti's day but a fresh gathering for the king's unsatisfied lust.
Wesley: Mordecai sat in the gate by office, advanced (he thinks) by Esther's favour.

debates.question: What is the 'second' gathering of virgins?

sides.position: a fresh gathering for the king's pleasure despite his having a queen
obscure — no clear reason after Esther's choice
a real second assembly showing how little the king's 'love' was worth

themes: the stage set for the plot

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: Esther still did Mordecai's commandment as when brought up with him; Ellicott, the verse meets the thought the king might replace her on learning her nation.
Gill: she had not shown her people, before or since her crowning — the Targum, though the king pressed her.
Henry: her continued obedience the ornament of her greatness — remembering benefactors, keeping the impressions of good education.

themes: the double thread of the deliverance

schools.summary: Ellicott takes up 'in those days,' names the threshold-keepers (Bigthan the Bigtha/Bigthana of 1:10; 6:2), and recalls Xerxes' actual murder by a guard and a chamberlain.
Clarke reports the Targum's motive — the two feared Esther would displace them for Mordecai — and thinks them Haman's creatures.
Gill: Mordecai sat in the king's gate, an officer at court.
Henry: God gives Mordecai a chance to serve the king, that he may later serve the Jews — the plot a step in the design of deliverance.
Keil and Delitzsch: the thing known to Mordecai, told to Esther, certified to the king in Mordecai's name; Ellicott, the influence thereby gained over the king.
Clarke follows Josephus — Barnabasus overheard the plot, told Mordecai, then Esther, then the king.
Gill gathers the traditions — Tarsian speech overheard, Josephus's Barnabazus, or the Targum's Holy Ghost.
Clarke reads the death as impaling and defends the book against the reproach that God's name never appears, citing the LXX addition at v.20.
Ellicott reads it as crucifixion (a Persian punishment for rebels) and the 'book of the chronicles' as the record Herodotus cites — where the king's sleepless night will relight on Mordecai.
Gill: on full proof the two conspirators suffered.

outliers.note: Turns the execution-notice into a defence against the old reproach that God's name never occurs in Esther, appealing to the Septuagint's addition at v.20.
